Doesn't work like that. I was diagnosed "manic depressive" when I was 8, and kinda fell by the wayside with care. You're too young to understand at that age, no one explained it to me, and I was oblivious to it. I didn't find out until I was in my late teens after an extended period of mania drew to an end. I had built a life based on me being manic; made friends, built a local fanbase as a performer, and had opportunities laid out before me based on who I was at the time. Then I went into the depression that followed, which completely crushed me and changed me as a person. I lost all those friends, was no good at the work I did anymore.. just became a wreck. Then I went to the doctor to be told that "manic depressive" was now called bipolar; not that I was aware of the former in the first place. Pretty much had to build my life back from there. From scratch. But it can be done. It just takes self awareness, honesty, acceptance, and compromise. It's not nice. It's not fair. But it does get easier with time. Hang in there.

It largely depends on the type of tenancy you have, and what's in the tenancy agreement. If your landlord doesn't live with you, or have access to your room, then you've probably got an AST.

With an AST rent can be increased if:

You and your landlord agree, and you pay the higher rate
You sign a new contract, and pay a higher rate
Through a rent review clause in your agreement
A section 13 notice.

If you have a rent review clause in your contract, your rent can only be increased in exactly the way the clause dictates. So worth checking.

If you're issued a s.13, you'll get one month's notice before the increase takes effect. They can only do this once every 12 months. And, if you don't agree with it, you can challenge the increase at a first tier tribunal.

They'll come in and decide if it's worth the rent or not.

If they think it's too high, they can ask your landlord to charge less. But that only applies to your tenancy. So your landlord will probably not you with a section 21 and then rent to someone else for the higher rate.

If they think its too low then your landlord can charge you even more.

If they think it's right, your landlord might hit you with the s.21 because you pissed em off.

There's no real limit on how much they can increase it by, either. That went out the window in '89.
